items.title: SOM completes first phase of Philadelphia train station restoration
items.summary:
Architecture studio SOM has completed the first phase of the renovation of the William H Gray III 30th Street Station in Philadelphia , USA, "breathing new life" into the 1930s beaux arts main train hall.

The project saw the renovation of the main train hall, a beaux arts Graham, Anderson, Probst & White building completed in 1931 with a grand limestone facade and Corinthian columns. It serves as a major transit hub for the Northeastern United States.

The hall is on the National Register of Historic Places, greatly restricting the changes that can be made to the structure and its interiors.

Keeping to the historic details, including the art deco chandeliers that hang from the tall ceilings, SOM restored the space with builder Gilbane through renovation and a series of specific interventions.

Chief among these was the moving of ticketing, bag drop-off, and other facilities that had been placed in the main train hall into a little-used northern wing of the building.

"Our restoration and repositioning presents an extraordinary opportunity to leverage the station's strengths, while breathing new life into this beloved building,” said SOM Partner Colin Koop. 

This move freed up more room for seating and through traffic in the main hall.

Working with retail partner Nelson Worldwide, SOM also revamped the concessions in the south concourse.

Lagoons will weave through new Egyptian city masterplanned by SOM 

SOM worked closely with US rail system operator Amtrak on the project, which includes offices for Amtrak in the upper levels of the building.

items.t: SOM completes first phase of Philadelphia train station restoration

items.title: Dezeen launches 20x20 project to identify the architects and designers to watch over the next 20 years
items.summary:
Today is Dezeen's 20th birthday, and to celebrate we launch our 20x20 project in partnership with Kohler. For the series we've asked 20 architects and designers who have had a major impact over the past 20 years to each select an architect or designer that they believe will have the biggest impact over the next 20 years.

Called 20x20 , the project aims to celebrate the past 20 years of Dezeen while looking forward to the names and faces we'll be seeing much more of in the next 20 years.

We'll be revealing the selected architects and designers on Dezeen over the next four weeks, getting to know them and their work in a series of interviews.

The series launches today with a profile of Russian-born, Paris-based designer Harry Nuriev , who was selected by Danish architect Bjarke Ingels.

He will be followed by the selections of Es Devlin, Faye Toogood, Francine Houbine, Frida Escobedo, Huberto Campana, Iris van herpen, Jeanne Gang, Kelly Wearstler, Lesley Lokko, Ma Yansong, Marc Newson, Mariam Kamara, Marina Tabassum, Nendo, Neri&Hu, Patricia Urquiola, Philippe Starck, Sabine Marcelis, Sou Fujimoto and Yasmeen Lari.

All of the interviews will be listed below as they are published:

Day 1: Harry Nuriev, selected by Bjarke Ingels

items.title: Meet Harry Nuriev, Bjarke Ingels' pick for the most influential designer of the next 20 years
items.summary:
BIG founder Bjarke Ingels has selected Harry Nuriev for Dezeen's 20x20 project in partnership with Kohler. In this interview , the Russian-born, Paris-based architect and designer explains how he constantly aims to reinvent himself and his work.

Nuriev established his studio, Crosby Studios , 12 years ago with the aim of shaking up the world of interior design .

"First, it came from this game of rejection," he told Dezeen from his house in Tuscany.

"Let's say everyone likes to use wood – I won't have any wood. If everyone likes beige or brown – I won't have beige or brown. People are confused with a material, so that's exactly the material I'm going to use."

"I'll bring exterior to interior, interior to exterior," he continued. "I'll mess everything. My colours will be inspired by fashion, my texture will be inspired by architecture."

"You can't be safe. You always have to risk."

BIG founder Bjarke Ingels selected Harry Nuriev for Dezeen's 20x20 project. Photo by Petra Kleis 

Over a decade later, the strategy appears to have worked. Nuriev was recently named Designer of the Year at French design show Maison&Objet and has a client list that many designers would envy. Among his recent works are a sofa for Balenciaga, a pop-up store for Skims, a reflecting pool for Gucci and a puffer-jacket-filled virtual sofa for Nike.

Now Ingels, arguably the world's best known architect, has selected him as the designer that he believes will have the biggest impact over the next 20 years, as part of our new series marking 20 years of Dezeen.

items.t: Meet Harry Nuriev, Bjarke Ingels' pick for the most influential designer of the next 20 years

For the project, SSdH wanted to focus on adaptation over replacement and aimed to work as much as possible with the existing warehouse structure. 

The studio designed a raised courtyard , a steel-mesh external stair tower and a double-height atrium to draw more natural light into the 770-square-metre space.

"We approached the project as an intervention within an existing building, rather than simply designing an interior," said Esrawe Studio founder Héctor Esrawe, who also co-founded Xinú .

"By introducing a continuous architectural structure that traverses its different levels, appearing and disappearing throughout the volume, we intended to generate a new perception of the original architecture," he told Dezeen.

items.summary:
Spanish design practice Isern Serra combined organic architectural forms with a vibrant colour palette for Circl, a fitness studio and matcha cafe located in Barcelona ’s historic Eixample district.

Set just below street level, the 180-square-metre space was designed to offer an escape from the busy city centre and contains an entrance cafe, reception area, changing rooms, bathrooms and a pilates studio.

Photographs 

Previous

“The project began with the idea of bringing together two worlds: pilates and matcha," Isern Serra told Dezeen. 

"Although different in nature, both share a common philosophy centred on wellbeing, balance and the connection between body and mind,” he continued. 

“Architecture plays an essential role in this experience, accompanying visitors on a gradual transition from the energy of the city towards a more intimate and introspective environment.” 

His studio introduced a series of colour-blocked spaces to guide customers through different phases of the interior, with colours that were specifically chosen to correspond to the function and tone of each area.

“This vision of wellbeing takes shape through a carefully choreographed sequence of spaces, where each change in level, colour and atmosphere guides users away from the bustle of the city and towards an increasingly introspective environment,” said Serra.

items.title: ESR x Craig & Karl Bring a Pocket Full of Joy to Everyday Technology
items.summary:
The objects we carry often reveal more about us than we realize. From the jewelry we wear to the accessories we keep within reach, even the smallest possessions become expressions of personal style. Yet as technology plays an increasingly central role in our lives, the devices we interact with most remain largely defined by their utility. Bringing more personality to these everyday essentials is the idea behind Pocket Full of Joy—a new collaboration between ESR , a consumer tech accessories brand, and creative duo Craig & Karl —which transforms phone cases and wallets into colorful, functional accessories.

Known for their vibrant compositions and playful iconography, Craig & Karl bring their distinctive visual language to a collection of iPhone cases and magnetic wallets. The collaboration draws upon the duo’s affinity for bold colors and familiar imagery, translating their graphic sensibilities into objects designed to accompany their owners throughout the day. The result is a collection that explores how artistic expression can become part of everyday life.

Across the collection, sticker-like illustrations, saturated hues, and expressive typography lend a sense of character to otherwise utilitarian surfaces. A collage of playful symbols evokes the spontaneity of a personal scrapbook, while the graphic “OK” design introduces a lighthearted note of optimism. Elsewhere, the cheerful “HI” motif transforms a magnetic wallet into a small, portable greeting. Each composition reflects Craig & Karl’s recognizable aesthetic while giving everyday accessories a more personal…

items.title: Photos reveal scale of Trump’s White House ballroom, drawing criticism
items.summary:
Earlier this month, Trump’s White House ballroom and military bunker laid its final structural steel beam, with politicians and critics weighing in on the scale of the project.

Recently taken images of the extension, which show the structure with massive concrete shear walls, steel beams, and columns, along with a partially enclosed roof structure, have drawn attention to the scale of the building.

No sign of its planned neoclassical ornamentation has yet been implemented.

The White House ballroom topped out earlier this month. Above photo by Aaron Butler Jr. Top photo by Philip Yabut 

Officially called the East Wing Modernization Project, the structure dwarfs the Executive Residence and West Wing.

Trump announced the laying of the last steel beam in the superstructure on 4 November, the day after the national midterm elections.

"This is a special structure," Trump said on a tour on 4 November, according to NBC News . "It’s going to be not only one of the biggest, but it’ll be the most beautiful ballroom, I think, anywhere in the world, and they’ve been trying to get it for 150 years.” 

It says everything about Donald Trump that his gilded ballroom dwarfs the size of the People's House—and it says everything about the American people that they repudiated him loudly and clearly last Tuesday. pic.twitter.com/ou23LpAes8 

— Hillary Clinton (@HillaryClinton) November 13, 2026 

Since then, there has been a renewed wave of criticism online over the project, ranging from outrage to humour.

items.title: Nike Tuned Air "a huge stride forward" in air-filled trainer design says innovation lead
items.summary:
Sportswear brand Nike  has unveiled the 3D-printed air bags that will be used for its next generation of air-filled trainers . In this interview, the brand's chief innovation, design & product officer Phil McCartney explains why it is a technological and performance advance.

"I see it personally as a revolution, not an evolution," McCartney told Dezeen from the LeBron James Innovation Center in Oregon . "It's a huge stride forward."

Tuned Air was designed to give Nike much greater control of how air is used within the midsole to provide cushioning and support. Using a combination of proprietary 3D printing and "selective lamination" allows Nike to create midsoles that perform in different ways under different parts of the foot.

Informed by the raised vibrant colours on magazine covers, the airbag is built up from layers of ink.

Nike has unveiled Nike Tuned Air 

"We can engineer the structure and tune the structure in the heel differently to the forefoot," said McCartney.

"We can also tune the height, so you can have a variety of different heights, and we can tune the structure inside."

Nike unveiled the technology and concept images for a running shoe today, and is planning for the first Nike Tuned Air trainer to be launched next year.

The trainers will be the first in what Nike sees as a third major generation of its air-filled shoes, since Nike CEO Phil Knight worked with inventor Frank Rudy to use a cushioning system filled with gas in the late 1970s.

Following the Nike Air Tailwind in 1978, Nike developed Air Max in the 1980s and Air Zoom in the 1990s.

items.title: Arcadia’s New Almeya Collection Marks A New Era of Flexible Design
items.summary:
Hybrid and remote work have changed what people expect from a modern workspace. No longer do people want fixed seating or single-purpose design. Instead, they are looking for modular, multi-use furniture that boosts productivity while maintaining comfort and style. When Chris and Jon Panichella set out to design their latest seating collection for Arcadia , they turned to everyday life for inspiration.

“The idea for Almeya began with a woman working from an inflatable raft at the beach,” the Panichellas explain. “She could recline and read in one position, then sit up and work in another—a simple moment that captured how much people now expect from their spaces: comfort, flexibility, and function. That observation became the very first concept sketch that eventually evolved into the Almeya offering we know today.”

Photography courtesy of Arcadia.

With a full family of products—including modular, lounge, work-lounge, benches, and occasional tables—the Almeya Collection offers a fluid experience that adapts to these modern shifts in productivity and collaboration. Across the series, soft, organic forms invite comfort and ease, while integrated tables, flexible configurations, and strategic power stations allow for both focus and sociability.

Almeya began with a single lounge chair and an integrated two-tiered side table. The idea was simple: the combination could function as a self-contained work island, with two separate surfaces, power access, and an optional rotating tablet. With this concept in mind, the Panichellas developed a standalone lounge chair, love seat, and…

items.title: Shisuo Design Office creates "surreal" rural house in China using salvaged steel
items.summary:
Jiang Deng Lu is a house in rural Anhui designed by Chinese studio Shisuo Design Office using stainless-steel offcuts salvaged from the client's own factory.

Described by Shisuo Design Office as a "surreal rural house", the compact building is raised partially on stilts to look as though it is floating above its sloped riverside site.

Drawings and photographs 

Previous 

Next

Close 

Floor plan

It sits beside the client's ancestral home and serves as both a memorial for his late father and a separate dwelling where his elderly mother can host visiting relatives.

"The client wanted to build a house beside the old family home, providing a comfortable place for his mother and relatives to gather and share meals during holidays," Shisuo Design Office told Dezeen.

"But beyond this practical need, there was a deeper emotional connection. The old house was left by his father, while the new one represented his own way of creating new memories for the family," it continued.

"We hoped the house would bring the family together more often, beyond just festive occasions."

Jiang Deng Lu's proportions were determined by the recycled stainless steel offcuts and unused windows salvaged for the project by the client, who is the owner of a stainless steel factory.

"The building’s geometry was strictly reverse-engineered from these salvaged materials," said Shisuo Design Office.

How are you feeling about the rapid dying of the light? Are you already sluggish and glum, poleaxed by the “polar vortex” or seasonal lurgy? That might be because you’re doing winter wrong: according to health psychologist Kari Leibowitz, writing in the Washington Post, we’d all benefit from a “winter transition week”.

Leibowitz, the author of a book, How to Winter, based on her time living in the Arctic, explains: “I intentionally clear out my calendar … say no to extra obligations, try to cancel or postpone unnecessary meetings and make time for rest and slowness.” During this time, she also recommends stocking up on tea, getting out thick socks, eating soup and planning little treats.

"As we began to conceive our first chapter of Casa Mouda, we knew we needed to start by recognizing some of the people who had already built so much of its foundation," said Chagoury Moudaber.

items.title: Eight highlights from this year's Sharjah Architecture Triennial

The third Sharjah Architecture Triennial focuses on the myriad ways architecture can be understood through the lens of anthropology. Here are our highlights from the event, including installations and exhibitions. 

Curated by anthropologist Vyjayanthi Rao, this year's edition was centred on the theme Architecture Otherwise: Building Civic Infrastructure for Collective Futures.

Rao said the 2026 Sharjah Architecture Triennial, which takes place over five months, will invite discourse about the different ways cities and urban life can be imagined.

Read:

Sharjah Architecture Triennial "to challenge the idea that architecture is just about iconic buildings" 

"Though I'm not an architect, I'm literally talking to students day in and day out about how they see the world, and how that translates into the practice," Rao told Dezeen. 

"Being an academic, you're always asked to define yourself in terms of your discipline," she continued. "It doesn't make sense to limit yourself, especially when you are in the practice of life." 

"You're learning from people about the ways in which they live – that's what I do as an anthropologist, and I think that's what a lot of architects do because they're inspired to build for people and the places that they inhabit and thrive in."

Read on for eight highlights from this year's Sharjah Architecture Triennial.

items.title: B2 Architecture turns North Korean defector testimonies into Prague exhibition
items.summary:
B2 Architecture has created the Life Behind the Walls exhibition in Prague , using a maze of red timber frames and translucent fabric to explore life in North Korea .

The 1,500-square-metre exhibition takes visitors from a bright, interactive installation designed around a children's book to a darkened gallery featuring portraits and testimonies from North Korean defectors.

B2 Architecture created an exhibition exploring life in North Korea 

B2 Architecture divided the installation into two contrasting environments. The first features a grid of red-painted timber beams, with large sheets of red and pink fabric suspended between the frames to create semi-transparent walls.

The structure forms a maze that visitors can explore, with glimpses of other rooms and activities visible through the fabric.

Red timber frames and translucent fabric form the exhibition maze 

Illustrated panels, games and interactive activities are fitted into the structure, while photographs by photographer Michal Huniewicz show North Korea as it is presented to the outside world.

Children are encouraged to navigate the maze independently and stop to draw, write and complete activities as they move through the installation.

The modular structure creates semi-transparent rooms 

The displays are based on Tota lítá, a children's book by North Korean studies scholar and writer Nina Špitálníková, which explains the principles of totalitarianism in language that is accessible to younger readers.

"Children are often given very little space within exhibition formats," B2 Architecture told Dezeen.…

They asked Pepper & Well to upgrade it and make it more accessible.

"There was an opportunity to make the space more comfortable and practical as they aged," said lead architect Andy Dal Pozzo.

The previous layout included a WC, an enclosed shower and a step-in plunge pool, all within a space just 3.5 metres long.

Pepper & Well's scheme removed the plunge, allowing space for a larger WC and for an open shower to be built in place of the old frosted-glass enclosure.

The defining move was the addition of a cast-concrete element that partitions the toilet and shower areas.

This incorporates an informal bench, allowing for seated showers if preferred.

The geometry of this element clearly references the house's exposed concrete structure, a rhythmic arrangement of concrete beams over concrete walls.

Designed to be durable and adaptable, Area combines aluminium columns, a panoply of tabletop options and concealed power.

items.title: Tant A Temps Design "restores the visual characteristics of Tang architecture" in Chinese cafe
items.summary:
Local practice Tant A Temps Design aimed to revive the aesthetics of the Tang Dynasty when designing the interiors for cafe Laibei 1087, located in a historical building in Xi'an , China .

The cafe sits inside the Beilin Museum , originally constructed in 1087 to preserve stone steles inscribed with Confucian philosophy and famous calligraphic works.

Plans and drawings

The timber columns and beams of the historic building were preserved, with the same approach extended into the cafe interiors. 

Guided by a "minimum intervention" and "zero damage" renovation strategy, Tant A Temps Design made every new addition detachable and reversible, which allowed the building's original features to remain untouched.

In the cafe, the furniture is suspended from wooden beams or arranged around columns to avoid direct contact with the original structures.

Tant A Temps Design also created tables, chairs and display cabinets with designs that draw from elements of the ancient building framework, such as the beams, columns and dougong brackets .

Lightweight and prefabricated materials and modular systems were used throughout the space.

For the main colour palette, Tant A Temps Design chose light green hues complemented by gold accents.

"The purpose of choosing this colour scheme is to restore the visual characteristics of Tang architecture – robust, imposing and richly coloured," the studio explained.

The Francine Houben-led architecture studio oversaw a complete retrofit of De Nederlandsche Bank, a 1968 structure that some had described as the nation's ugliest building.

The building was further complicated by later extensions, which included an extra storey above the low-rise main building and a cylindrical 14-storey tower built alongside the original central tower.

Mecanoo's transformation was enabled by the relocation of gold reserves and banknote operations to a location in Zeist.

The building is located in the centre of Amsterdam

items.title: Kohler's gut-health tracker clips onto the toilet bowl
items.summary:
American bathroom brand Kohler has created Dekoda, a health tracker specifically for the toilet , through its spin-off venture, Kohler Health.

Dekoda is designed to be discreet and intuitive, clipping to the side of the toilet bowl to give insights on gut health and hydration levels, and to detect the presence of blood.

In the emerging toilet-based health tracker market, it is the first device capable of blood detection, which it does through sensors developed at Kohler Health that identify haemoglobin.

Photographs 

Previous 

Next 

Photographs

Close 

The company said the device is particularly useful for older individuals or those with chronic gut illnesses, who need to track their symptoms as part of their disease management programmes.

“When we developed Dekoda, our goal was to give people the tools to listen to their bodies, track meaningful results over time, and take charge of their own wellness journey," said Kohler Health managing director Nora Tophof.

"It’s important to realise that the human eye is only capable of seeing so much – and trace amounts of blood or other issues are not always apparent," she continued. "Subtle biological markers, such as microscopic blood or early signs of dehydration, often go unnoticed." 

"Dekoda works quietly behind the scenes to capture those crucial clues, giving people clear, objective data they can use to help shape behaviours or share with their doctor," Tophof said.

People with dementia often forget to drink or lose the feeling of thirst, while people with gut diseases such as Crohn's usually need to track their…
items.t: Kohler's gut-health tracker clips onto the toilet bowl

items.title: Arudeko transforms discarded wool into paper-like material
items.summary:
Mexican design studio Arudeko has developed Bianni, a paper-like material made from colourful waste wool , which can be sculpted into everything from lampshades to room dividers.

Sourced from the off-cuts of handmade carpets and cushions crafted by local weaving communities in Teotitlán del Valle, Mexico, Arudeko saw the potential to use the surplus material and save it from being discarded.

Bianni is a paper-like material crafted from colourful waste wool 

Photographs 

Previous 

Next 

Photographs

Close 

The material can be sculpted into lampshades 

The customisable textile – named Bianni – was made by weaving together wool with recycled paper. 

Skilled local artisans initially wove the discarded dyed wool onto a pedal loom, then, using cotton threads, wove strips of recycled paper crafted by local papermakers into the material.

The result is a translucent, flexible textile that can be crafted into diverse objects, from lampshades to decorative headboard panels, room dividers and wall art.

"Through exploring the material's qualities, we discovered its potential, particularly the way light revealed colours that had been hidden within the paper, almost like a secret waiting to be uncovered," Arudeko co-founder and CEO Denisse Arnaiz told Dezeen.

"Once the paper was woven, I began observing how it behaved as a textile," added Arnaiz. 

"Its translucency was what ultimately inspired us to explore its use in lighting. However, the material has many other possible applications."

items.title: The Peralta D Supercar Is Literally Sculpted From Copper
items.summary:
For the last century or so, ever since wood fell out of style, the bodies of most automobiles have been made from a few tried-and-true materials: carbon fiber, fiberglass, aluminum, and steel, with the metals proving most popular. The choices are a balancing act, forcing carmakers to weigh price, safety, convenience, and appearance to determine which substance makes the most sense for the masses.

Photography courtesy of GFG Style

But what if you didn’t have to worry about such concerns? What if cost was no object, practicality a formality, and there was no need to cater to the wants of more than one owner? Well, that was the lucky circumstance designer Fabrizio Giugiaro, founder and CEO of GFG Style , found himself in when creating the Peralta D, a gran turismo with a body made of hand-hammered copper. 

Photography courtesy of GFG Style

“It was a proposal I made to the client, Carlos Peralta,” Giugiaro says. The duo had worked together before on the design house’s first one-off automobile, the spitshine-polished 1980s-esque Peralta S . For the follow-up, Giugiaro wanted to draw a deeper connection to the owner. As an industrialist, Peralta has business interests involving copper, so Giugiaro suggested it as the material.

Photography courtesy of GFG Style

Giugiaro’s name is well known in the automotive world. His father, Giorgetto Giugiaro , is a master of clean-line designs—he penned the DeLorean DMC-12, the BMW M1, the original Lotus Esprit, and the first Volkswagen Golf. The senior Giugiaro’s career has included work for Ferrari, Lamborghini, Bugatti, and many more…
items.t: The Peralta D Supercar Is Literally Sculpted From Copper

items.title: Friday Five With Shaina Tabak: Art, Architecture, and the Spaces Between
items.summary:
Though she’s still pursuing her MFA in Visual Arts at Columbia University, artist Shaina Tabak is hardly a newcomer to the art world. The RISD graduate, who earned her BFA in furniture design, already has more than 20 exhibitions under her belt. Now she’s adding curator to her résumé with 260 Madison , an artist-run exhibition bringing together more than 50 artists across a former Duane Reade storefront and a 23,000-square-foot office floor above it in Midtown Manhattan.

Tabak’s own work is equally expansive. Drawing on history, technology, and materiality, she explores the relationship between the digital and physical worlds, often starting with digitally modeled forms that she translates into sculptures through hands-on processes such as cutting, perforation, lamination, and extrusion.

‘On Certainties (streetlight)’ (2026) by Anthony Discenza and ‘Arbor Armor’ (2015–2026) by Yasue Maetake on display at ‘260 Madison.’ Photography courtesy of Shaina Tabak.

But her interest in materials extends beyond their physical properties. She also sees them as records of labor, manufacturing, extraction, and use. Her work examines contemporary material culture through a historical lens, imagining how the things made and valued today might be understood generations from now. As she puts it, her sculptures are “less concerned with imagining the future than with creating historical distance from the present.”

That perspective comes through in her recent work, which examines the increasingly blurred line between looking and shopping. In her Brooklyn studio, the Queens-born artist has…
items.t: Friday Five With Shaina Tabak: Art, Architecture, and the Spaces Between

items.title: Cold Plunges Are Finding a New Place in Residential Design
items.summary:
Once relegated to backyards and home gyms, cold plunges are finding a new place in residential design. As the wellness practice grows in popularity, homeowners are increasingly looking to incorporate cold therapy directly into their bathrooms, transforming what was once a standalone piece of fitness equipment into an integrated feature of the home.

The interest goes beyond athletic recovery. Cold-water immersion has been associated with potential benefits ranging from reduced muscle soreness to improved sleep and stress management, although research into its broader health effects remains limited. Still, the appeal is evident. According to Houzz’s 2024 Summer Trends Report , searches for “cold plunge” increased 74% year over year, while searches for “indoor sauna” rose 69%.

In the Heber, Utah, residence by Berg Design Studio, Hydro Systems’ Marquis bathtub demonstrates how traditional freestanding tubs can accommodate emerging wellness technologies, including cold plunging. Photography by Steve C. Wilson.

That interest reflects a larger shift toward wellness-focused residential spaces. The company’s 2026 report found that searches for “wellness room” had increased 164%, suggesting that homeowners are thinking more intentionally about how their environments can support relaxation and well-being.

For interior designers, these changing priorities are introducing new considerations into residential projects. Arizona-based designer Stephanie Larsen , who incorporates cold plunges, infrared saunas, and integrated aromatherapy systems into her work, has seen clients place…
items.t: Cold Plunges Are Finding a New Place in Residential Design
